p: Paul's phrase peri de ton pneumatikon can mean 'about spiritual gifts' or 'about spiritual people'.
b: The Greek pneumatikon is a genitive plural that can be neuter (spiritual things, gifts) or masculine (spiritual persons). Most translations choose 'gifts' because Paul goes on to list gifts, and because 12:4 switches to the different word charismata. But Paul's later words 'if anyone thinks he is a prophet, or spiritual' (14:37) show that 'spiritual people' was a Corinthian boast, and 14:1 uses the neuter plural for 'gifts of the Spirit'. The Plain keeps the wider 'spiritual matters' so both readings stay open. The phrase 'now about' also marks an answer to a question the Corinthians had sent in a letter (7:1; 8:1; 16:1).

t: Mute idols, and the living God who speaks
p: The Old Testament mocks idols as mouths that cannot speak; Paul uses the same contrast for his Gentile readers.
b: Isaiah, Habakkuk and the Psalms all make fun of idols as things with a mouth that never speaks (Psalm 115:5; Habakkuk 2:18). Paul turns that Jewish argument on his readers' own past. Corinth and its neighbors had famous speaking places: the oracle of Apollo at Delphi, across the Gulf of Corinth, where a priestess spoke in a trance, and cults of Dionysus and Cybele known for ecstatic behavior. Some Corinthians may have thought speaking in a trance proved the Spirit was present. Paul does not deny that they had strong religious experiences before. He says that experience alone does not tell them whose power is at work, and gives them a test in the next verse.

t: 'Jesus is under a curse': who said it?
p: Nobody knows who in Corinth, if anyone, ever cursed Jesus. Scholars offer at least five answers.
b: The Greek is anathema Iesous, 'Jesus is accursed.' The views: (1) Jews, or Jewish opponents, who cursed Jesus in the synagogue (the hanged man is under God's curse, Deuteronomy 21:23; compare Galatians 3:13); (2) a group of Corinthians in trance who said it (the view of some older scholars); (3) a group who split the human Jesus from the heavenly Christ (Schmithals); (4) a pagan or Jewish test that the Corinthians had faced in court; (5) a made-up example: even in ecstasy, the Spirit of God never leads anyone to say it. Fee and Thiselton both list these and decide that no one can be sure. The Plain says 'under a curse' to keep the sense of a person handed over to God's judgment.

p: 'Jesus is Lord' was the first Christian confession, and in Greek it used the word the Septuagint uses for YHWH.
b: The Greek kyrios Iesous is the shortest creed in the New Testament. It is linked with baptism and with the Spirit also in Romans 10:9 and Philippians 2:11. The Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament, uses kyrios for the divine name, so the confession placed Jesus at the right hand of God. In Corinth it also set a rival claim: 'Caesar is lord' and the many 'lords' of the cults (8:5). Larry Hurtado argues that this devotion to Jesus began very early among Jewish believers and was not a late Gentile addition. Paul's point here is that this confession, not any dramatic experience, is the mark of the Spirit.

p: Charisma is a word built on charis, 'grace': something given freely, not earned.
b: Charisma (plural charismata) is rare before Paul. It means a favor or gift of grace. Paul uses it for God's gift of eternal life (Romans 6:23), for his own unmarried or married state (7:7), and, in these chapters, for abilities given for the good of the church. Each of the three words in 12:4-6 has a different emphasis: charismata stresses that they are gifts; diakoniai ('services', 12:5) that they are for serving others; energemata ('workings', 12:6) that God's power is at work. Paul does not set up three kinds of ability. The three words describe the same activity from three sides.

t: Spirit, Lord, God: a threefold pattern
p: Verses 4-6 name Spirit, Lord and God in turn, a pattern later churches used in talking about the Trinity.
b: Paul writes 'the same Spirit' (12:4), 'the same Lord' (12:5), 'the same God' (12:6). He is not teaching the doctrine of the Trinity here; his point is that one source stands behind every gift. But the pattern, with the Spirit, Christ and the Father working together, is one of the places the later church looked when it spoke of three who are one. Compare the threefold blessing in 2 Corinthians 13:14 and the order in Ephesians 4:4-6. Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant writers all cite the verse in this way; scholars of every kind agree that the doctrine is a later and careful working out of what Paul assumes here.

a: a way of showing the Spirit
p: The Spirit is said to be 'shown' in the gifts, and the gifts are for the benefit of all.
b: The Greek phanerosis means a bringing into the open. The Spirit is invisible, but gifts make him known. The genitive 'of the Spirit' is read two ways: the Spirit is what is shown (most commentators), or the Spirit is the one who shows something else. Then comes the test of every gift: pros to sympheron, 'for the common benefit' or 'for what is advantageous.' The same word appears in 6:12 and 10:23, 33, where Paul sets what 'helps' people against what is merely allowed. In Corinth, where some used spiritual gifts to rank themselves, 'for the common good' is the rule that ends the argument.

t: 'A word of wisdom' and 'a word of knowledge'
p: Two of the gifts have been read as supernatural insight, as skilled teaching, or as speeches fitted to the moment.
b: The Greek is logos sophias and logos gnoseos. Wisdom and knowledge were Corinthian favorites (1:17 to 2:16; 8:1). Readings: (1) Spirit-given insight into a situation or a hidden fact, as Pentecostal and charismatic writers often hold; (2) the gift of explaining and teaching the gospel, as many older commentators took it; (3) a spoken message in which wisdom or knowledge is expressed, nothing more specific being known (Fee). Paul gives no definition because the Corinthians knew what he meant. Notice that the first two gifts in the list are speech, and the list ends with tongues and their interpretation.

t: Both words are plural: 'gifts of healings'
p: Paul writes 'gifts of healings', with both words in the plural, as if each healing were its own gift.
b: The Greek charismata iamaton has two plurals. Some commentators think each healing is a separate gift, given for each occasion, rather than a person who holds the gift of healing as a standing office. The same plurals occur in 12:28 and 12:30. The New Testament elsewhere shows healing by apostles (Acts 3:1-10), by Philip (Acts 8:7) and by the elders anointing with oil (James 5:14-15). Churches differ on whether healing is still given in this way; Catholics and Orthodox pray for the sick in the sacrament of anointing, and Pentecostals and many charismatics expect healing in answer to prayer.

p: Paul ranks prophecy highest of the speaking gifts (14:1); scholars disagree on how authoritative it was.
b: Three main views. (1) Prophecy was a spontaneous word from God, given to a person in the meeting and open to being tested; it could be mixed with human error (Wayne Grudem). (2) It carried the same authority as the Old Testament prophets, and so ended once the apostles' writings were complete (many cessationists). (3) It was inspired preaching, applying Scripture to the moment (Calvin, and many Reformed teachers). Paul says prophecy is partial (13:9) and must be weighed (14:29). The first view takes this as the mark of an ordinary, fallible gift. The second reads the same verses as true of the gift while it lasted, and reads 'the complete' of 13:10 as the finished Scripture that ends it. The third takes weighing as the way a congregation tests a sermon against Scripture. Acts shows prophets such as Agabus foretelling events (Acts 11:28; 21:10-11). Early Christian prophecy outside the New Testament is in the Didache, chapters 11 to 13.
r: 1 Corinthians 14:29; Acts 11:28; Acts 21:10; Ephesians 2:20; Ephesians 4:11; 1 Thessalonians 5:20

p: The gift of 'discerning' or 'sorting out' spirits is the check on prophecy.
b: The Greek diakrisis pneumaton means a sorting out, a judging between. It is the sister of the command to 'weigh' prophecies in 14:29 (same root, diakrino). Possible meanings: judging whether a prophetic message comes from the Spirit of God, from another spirit, or from the speaker's own mind; or judging whether someone who speaks 'in the Spirit' is truly doing so (12:3). First John 4:1 and 1 Thessalonians 5:21 give the same advice: test everything. The plural 'spirits' reflects the ancient belief that spirits of various kinds could speak through a person.

p: In Acts, tongues are languages hearers understand; in Corinth they are speech that needs an interpreter.
b: The Greek glossai means 'tongues' and 'languages.' Views: (1) Real human languages the speaker never learned, as at Pentecost (Acts 2:4-11), where the crowd heard their own languages. (2) A prayer language, speech that does not belong to any human language, which Paul sets in 14:2 as speaking 'not to people but to God.' (3) The 'languages of angels' of 13:1, as in the Jewish Testament of Job, where Job's daughters are given sashes that let them sing in the dialect of the angels. (4) Ecstatic speech like that known in Greek religion, though Paul distinguishes it from the Spirit's gift by its use for the church. Most scholars hold that Acts and Corinth describe a related gift; some separate them.

t: The body as a picture of a city
p: Greek and Roman writers used 'the body' to urge rich and poor to stay together; Paul gives the picture a new twist.
b: The Roman historian Livy tells how Menenius Agrippa calmed the common people of Rome, who had walked out on the senators, by telling them a story of stomach and limbs: if the limbs starve the belly, they starve themselves (Livy, History of Rome 2.32). Other writers, Stoic and political, used a body to urge harmony. Margaret Mitchell argues that Paul is using this well-known device in a letter that is mostly an appeal for unity. Two differences: Paul says the body is 'Christ,' not a city, and he reverses the usual advice. In the ordinary use of the story, the lowly are told to accept their place. Paul tells the more honored members to value the weaker ones (12:22-25).

t: 'So also is the Christ': a body or a picture?
p: Is the church like a body, or is it, in some real sense, the body of Christ?
b: Paul does not say 'so also is the church' but 'so also is the Christ,' and the Plain keeps that wording without choosing among the views. Views: (1) A figure of speech: the church is like a body, as Greek authors said of cities (Conzelmann, Fee). (2) A real union: believers are joined to Christ and so to each other, as 6:15 suggests ('your bodies are members of Christ'). The Catholic Church teaches this in Pius XII's encyclical on the Mystical Body of Christ (1943) and in Lumen Gentium; the Orthodox speak of the church as Christ's body in the eucharist; Lutheran and Reformed writers affirm union with Christ without always using the word 'mystical.' (3) A play on Christ as the one in whom all are baptized (12:13), the 'corporate Christ' (C. F. D. Moule). The argument of 12:14-26 works with either.

t: 'Baptized in one Spirit': water, Spirit, or both?
p: The verse is the main text in the churches' arguments about 'baptism in the Spirit.'
b: The Greek en heni pneumati can be 'in one Spirit' (the Spirit is the element in which the baptism happens) or 'by one Spirit' (the Spirit is the one who baptizes). Four readings. (1) Conversion-initiation: all believers receive the Spirit at the start of Christian life (James Dunn; many Reformed and Baptist writers). (2) Water baptism, with the Spirit given in it (Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Anglican writers). (3) Christ is the baptizer and the Spirit the element (the Pentecostal view that 12:13 is about salvation, while 'baptism in the Spirit' as power for service is a different experience, taught from Acts). (4) A picture, with no reference to a rite. Note that Paul says 'all of us,' including the very Corinthians he is scolding.

a: Jews or Greeks, slaves or free people
p: The pairs Jew and Greek, slave and free appear again in Galatians 3:28 and Colossians 3:11.
b: 'Greek' here means any non-Jew, as in Romans 1:16. Paul lists the two great divisions of his world: religion and nation (Jew and Greek), and law and status (slave and free). The Galatians list adds a third, male and female (Galatians 3:28), and Colossians drops it and adds 'barbarian.' Paul does not say that the differences vanished; he writes of slaves in 7:21-24 and still speaks of Jews as Jews. His claim is that all are in the same body by the same Spirit, so that none of the divisions decides who belongs. In Corinth, where the rich and the poor ate separately at the Lord's meal (11:21), the point was not abstract.

a: given a drink of one Spirit
p: 'Drink' brings in pictures of the desert rock, the prophets' promise of poured-out water, and, for some, the cup.
b: The verb potizo means 'to give a drink to' or 'to water' a plant (3:6-8 uses it for Apollos watering). The Old Testament pictures the Spirit as water poured on dry ground (Isaiah 44:3; Joel 2:28). Paul has just used the desert rock that gave Israel drink, 'that rock was the Christ' (10:4). Some interpreters, ancient and modern, have heard an allusion to the cup of the Lord's Supper (10:16; 11:25). Calvin, in his commentary on the verse, is usually read as taking it as a second picture of the same truth: the Spirit is poured on us as water on a thirsty field. The Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus add 'into' (eis), 'drink into one Spirit,' behind the King James 'made to drink into one Spirit' (see the variant). The addition does not change the meaning in a major way.

t: The parts we would not show
p: Paul uses a delicate phrase for the private parts of the body; his point is that care, not display, gives honor.
b: The Greek aschemona ('unpresentable') is a polite word for the private parts. Clothing, Paul says, gives them 'extra' euschemosyne (decency, comeliness). The argument runs against ordinary Greek ranking: people at the dinner table or in the courts gave the front seat and the best cloth to the strong. In the body, he says, we do the opposite: we cover and protect the parts that cannot protect themselves. In Corinth, where the wealthy ate their fill while the poor went hungry at the Lord's Supper (11:21-22) and the educated looked down on the uneducated (1:26-29), the picture was a direct rebuke.

p: The verb is the one used for mixing wine and water in a bowl.
b: The Greek synekerasen is used in Greek for blending wine with water, and for putting different things together so that they become one. God, Paul says, did the blending, and he gave extra honor to the member that lacked it. In Corinth, honor was something people spent money and effort to win (Paul's own honor is under test in chapter 9). Here Paul reverses the usual idea: honor is not earned by the strong but given by God to the weak. This is the same pattern as 1:27-28, where God chose 'the foolish' and 'the weak' to shame the wise and the strong.

t: Three lists of gifts, three orders
p: Paul's lists of gifts are not the same: 12:8-10 has nine, 12:28 has eight, and Romans 12:6-8 has seven.
b: The lists overlap but never repeat. Only prophecy appears on all four lists (Romans 12:6-8; 1 Corinthians 12:8-10; 12:28; Ephesians 4:11). Teaching is on three of them, since it is not in 12:8-10. Only here are 'acts of help' and 'acts of steering' found. Most scholars take the lists as samples, not as a complete catalogue. The ranking 'first, second, third' in 12:28 puts apostles first as founders (3:10; Ephesians 2:20), prophets second, teachers third. The other gifts come after the word 'then,' unranked. Orthodox and Catholic writers connect the order with the later offices of bishop, presbyter and teacher; many Protestants hold that the three early offices are no longer given in the same way.

p: The Greek word comes from the pilot of a ship.
b: Kybernesis (plural here) comes from kybernetes, the steersman of a ship. It appears only here in the New Testament. In the Greek Old Testament it is used in Proverbs 1:5 for the 'guidance' the wise person acquires. It is the root of our word 'govern.' The gift is probably leadership and administration: seeing where the church should go and keeping it on course. Later commentators often took the word to mean the work of bishops and other rulers. Paul gives no job title; he gives the activity, and he puts it after healing and 'helping,' which suggests it was a service, not a rank.

p: The Greek question uses me, which expects the answer no. That bears on the Pentecostal teaching about tongues.
b: Each question in 12:29-30 begins with me, which in Greek expects 'No.' Paul says: do all speak in tongues? Of course not. Pentecostal teaching, as in the Assemblies of God's Statement of Fundamental Truths, holds that speaking in tongues is the first outward sign of being baptized in the Holy Spirit (the Acts pattern), and 12:30 is then read as about a different thing, the gift of tongues exercised in public for the church. Others (Baptist, Reformed, Catholic, Orthodox, and also some Pentecostal teachers) read 12:30 plainly: there is no requirement that every Christian speak in tongues. See the card on this verse.

a: Be eager for the greater gifts
p: The Greek verb can be read as a command ('be eager') or as a statement ('you are eager').
b: Zeloute has the same form in the command and in the statement. Most translations take it as a command, as the Plain does, and read 12:31 as a turn toward chapter 14, which repeats the verb as a command in 14:1 and 14:39. A few commentators take it as a statement: 'but you are eager for the greater gifts,' a mild rebuke of the Corinthians' competing, with 'a way beyond measure' (kath' hyperbolen) as the correction. The Plain also keeps the small Greek word eti, 'besides, still,' as 'And besides this.'

a: languages of humans and of angels
p: Does Paul speak in hyperbole, or did some in Corinth speak a heavenly language?
b: Views: (1) Exaggeration: Paul piles up impossible examples (all knowledge, all faith, giving away everything) and 'tongues of angels' is one more (Fee, Garland). (2) A real claim by some Corinthians that they spoke the speech of angels, which Paul does not deny but ranks below love (some scholars read 14:2 this way). Jewish writings did describe angels as speaking their own languages: the Testament of Job has Job's daughters speaking in the 'dialect of the angels' (chapters 48 to 50), and the Dead Sea Scrolls have angels praising God in song. Paul speaks of 'unspeakable words' heard in paradise in 2 Corinthians 12:4. Either way, even the best speech is empty without love.

p: Agape was a plain Greek word for love, not a special 'holy' one; its meaning comes from how Paul describes it.
b: A popular teaching says agape is 'God's unconditional love' and a different word from philia (friendship love) and eros (desire). The Greek Old Testament uses agapao for Amnon's lust for Tamar (2 Samuel 13:15, Septuagint) and 2 Timothy 4:10 uses it of Demas' love for this world, so the word is not holy by itself. The word became Christian because Paul and the others filled it with Christ's self-giving. The Plain renders it 'love' as the site's terms require. Here the content is in the portrait of 13:4-7, not in the vocabulary. In John 21:15-17 the two verbs are used in turn without any clear difference.

p: Cymbals were loud, and in Greek religion they belonged to the noisy cults of Cybele and Dionysus.
b: The Greek chalkos echon is 'sounding bronze,' perhaps a gong, a bronze vessel that rings, or a horn. The kymbalon alalazon is a cymbal that 'clangs.' Cymbals appear in the Old Testament in the Temple music (Psalm 150:5), but in Greek and Roman religion they were famous in the cults of Cybele and Dionysus, where loud music was used to bring on ecstasy. A Corinthian who had come out of those cults (12:2) would have heard Paul's meaning: speech full of power but empty of love is just another cult noise. Paul does not insult tongues here; he says that without love they are only sound.

p: A Jewish expression for doing the impossible; Jesus used it too.
b: 'Uprooter of mountains' was a Jewish expression for a teacher who could solve impossible difficulties in the law; the Babylonian Talmud uses it of a rabbi in Berakhot 64a. Jesus used the same idea of faith in Matthew 17:20 and Mark 11:23. Whether Paul knew that saying of Jesus is debated, but the picture is a common one. The point of 13:2 is the order of gifts: prophecy, knowledge and faith were prized in Corinth (12:8-9), yet Paul says even the faith that does miracles is nothing without love.

t: 'Give away': to feed bit by bit
p: The Greek verb psomizo means to feed with morsels, so Paul pictures giving until nothing is left.
b: Psomizo comes from psomion, a scrap of bread. It means to feed by small portions: give away all I own, a morsel at a time, to the hungry. Paul pictures giving to the poor as the highest act of generosity and says it still counts for nothing without love. The next clause is a variant in the manuscripts (see the variant on 'so that I can boast'). Giving was the glory of the rich in Corinth, where benefactors (patrons) won honor by gifts to the city. Paul may be pointing at that custom: you can get honor from giving without having love.

p: This is the word the Greek Old Testament uses for God's patience, now used of love.
b: Makrothymei means 'is long-tempered.' In the Greek Old Testament the related adjective describes the LORD in Exodus 34:6 ('slow to anger,' Hebrew erek appayim, 'long of nose'), one of the most quoted lines of the Old Testament (Numbers 14:18; Psalm 103:8; Jonah 4:2). Paul does not name God as the one who loves like this, but a Jewish reader would hear God's character in the list. The verbs of 13:4 are mostly about how love treats another person whose conduct is trying: it waits, and it acts kindly. The same root is rendered 'patience' in the list of the Spirit's fruit in Galatians 5:22, where the word stands as a noun; the Plain says 'slow to anger' here because the verbs of 13:4 describe how love acts toward a person who is trying. The second verb, chrestenetai ('acts with kindness'), is rare and may have been formed by Paul.

a: count up the harm done to it
p: The Greek logizomai is a bookkeeping word: love does not enter wrongs in a ledger.
b: Logizetai to kakon literally 'counts the evil.' The verb logizomai is Paul's accounting word, used of counting faith as righteousness (Romans 4:3) and of God not counting sins against people (2 Corinthians 5:19; Romans 4:8). Zechariah 8:17 uses similar words when it warns against planning evil against a neighbor. Here the sense is that love does not keep a record of what has been done to it, to bring out later. In Corinth, where people sued one another in the city courts (6:1-8) and the factions each kept a score (1:12), the phrase was close to home.

p: The verb stegei is built on the word for a roof, so it can mean cover, shelter or bear up.
b: Stego comes from stege, 'roof.' It can mean 'to cover' (as a roof covers), 'to keep out' or 'to bear what falls on you.' Readings: (1) Love puts up with all things (most translations). (2) Love covers over what is shameful in others, as in Proverbs 10:12, 'love lays a cover over all wrongdoing,' and 1 Peter 4:8. (3) Love keeps confidence and does not gossip. (4) Love protects. The Plain says 'covers' to keep the roof picture and the link with Proverbs. The same verb appears in 9:12 (Paul 'puts up with' everything rather than hinder the gospel).

p: The Greek verb means 'fall': love does not fall, give way or run out.
b: Most translations say love 'never fails.' The Greek pipto is 'falls,' as a building or a defeated soldier falls. The Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus read ekpipto, 'falls off, drops away,' which is the reading behind the King James 'never faileth' (see the variant). The contrast is with the verbs of the next phrases, which say that prophecies and knowledge will be 'set aside' and tongues will 'stop.' Love is the one thing that stays standing when everything else is gone. This is why Paul can set it in the middle of the letter's long discussion of gifts: the gifts are for now, and love is for always.

p: Prophecy and knowledge are 'set aside' by someone else, but tongues 'stop' by themselves; some read this as important.
b: The first and third verbs ('will be set aside,' katargethesontai) are passive: something will end them. The second, pausontai, is a middle-voice form. Some cessationist writers argue that it means tongues will cease on their own, before the others, perhaps by the end of the apostolic age (R. L. Thomas). Most grammarians reply that Greek has many verbs that appear only in the middle form with a plain active sense ('they will stop'), and that the contrast carries no weight; the same lines do not say when (D. A. Carson, Fee, Thiselton). The question of when tongues stop depends on what 'the complete' of 13:10 is, and on the rest of the New Testament.

p: What is 'the complete' (to teleion)? The answer decides what the verse says about the gifts today.
b: The Greek to teleion is neuter: 'the complete,' 'the perfect,' 'the mature.' (1) The return of Christ and the age to come, when we see 'face to face' (13:12); the view of most scholars and of Calvin, Fee, Thiselton and Carson. (2) The completed New Testament, so that tongues and prophecy ended when the canon was complete (Robert Thomas and many cessationists). (3) The church's maturity (the church 'grown up,' as in Ephesians 4:13). (4) Heaven, the state after death. The cessationist case on view (1) is made from other passages, such as Ephesians 2:20 and Hebrews 2:3-4, not from this verse. Continuationists say that 'face to face' and 'fully known' cannot refer to the canon. See the card.

p: Ancient mirrors were usually polished metal, which gave a blurred and reversed image.
b: A mirror in Paul's day was normally a polished disk of bronze, silver or a similar alloy, and its image was dim and slightly distorted. Glass mirrors existed, but they were rare and small. Paul's picture is that today we see an indirect image of the truth, not the thing itself. Two other readings: the mirror is the gospel itself, in which we see Christ's glory (2 Corinthians 3:18); or the image is of prophecy, which in Numbers 12:6-8 is said to be given 'in riddles' to ordinary prophets but 'face to face' to Moses.

a: what we see is a riddle
t: 'Not in riddles': Moses and the prophets
p: Paul's words 'riddle' and 'face to face' recall what God says of Moses in Numbers 12.
b: In Numbers 12:6-8 God says that he speaks to other prophets in dreams and visions, but to Moses 'mouth to mouth, openly and not in riddles.' The Greek Old Testament uses the same word as Paul for 'riddle' (ainigma). Moses seeing God 'face to face' is told in Exodus 33:11 and Deuteronomy 34:10. Paul says that for now every believer is in the position of the ordinary prophet, seeing through a riddle; only at the end will all see as Moses did. The line 'known as I have been known' echoes 8:3 ('if anyone loves God, that person is known by him') and Galatians 4:9.
r: Numbers 12:8; Exodus 33:11; Deuteronomy 34:10; 1 Corinthians 8:3; Galatians 4:9; 1 John 3:2

p: Paul puts the same three virtues together in several letters.
b: The three appear together in 1 Thessalonians 1:3 and 5:8, Romans 5:1-5, Galatians 5:5-6, Colossians 1:4-5 and (in a different order) Ephesians 4:2-5. They seem to have been a stock summary of Christian life. Here Paul claims that all three last, not only love. Readings: (1) They remain in the sense of lasting into the age to come, though faith and hope change when they are fulfilled. (2) They remain for now, unlike the gifts. The Plain's 'But now' keeps the Greek nuni ('now'), on which the temporal readings depend: it can mean 'in the present time' or 'as things stand once the gifts are set aside.' The ranking is clear: love is the greatest. Augustine took 'love' to be the one thing that will remain even in the vision of God.

p: Paul uses a hunting word: chase love, then be eager for gifts.
b: The Greek dioko means 'to chase, pursue,' used of hunters and runners. In Paul it is a strong word for a settled goal (Romans 14:19; 1 Thessalonians 5:15; Philippians 3:12, 14). The verse joins chapters 13 and 14: love first, then gifts. Chapter 13 is not an interruption in the argument. It is the center of it, between the gifts as the Spirit's work (12) and the use of two gifts in the meeting (14). Paul gives two commands: chase love, and be eager (zeloute) for the gifts, with prophecy as the first desire, because it builds up (14:3-5).

a: speaks not to people but to God
p: Greek religion had ecstatic prophecy; some think Corinth borrowed tongues from it. The evidence is thin.
b: At Delphi the priestess of Apollo, the Pythia, gave oracles in a trance, and Plato speaks of a 'divine madness' that gives prophecy (Phaedrus 244). Virgil describes the Sibyl as wild and foaming (Aeneid 6). Some scholars have said that Corinthian tongues came from such cults. Christopher Forbes argues that the parallels are weaker than often claimed: the Pythia's words were intelligible, and Greek writers do not describe a language with no meaning. The Jewish background (Numbers 11:25-29; 1 Samuel 10:5-6; 19:20-24) shows prophets in ecstatic states, and Paul's own words about the Spirit's groans (Romans 8:26) also have no words. Paul says tongues are a gift of the Spirit, not a borrowed custom, but he judges them by their use.

p: The Greek says no one 'hears' him; as in English, to hear can mean to understand.
b: The Greek verb akouei is 'hears.' Paul does not mean that the sound cannot be heard. He means no one grasps it, as in Mark 4:33 or Acts 9:7 on a different matter. The Plain keeps 'mysteries' for mysteria, the same word as 'mysteries' in 4:1 and 'mystery' in 2:7 and 15:51 and in Romans 11:25, where the site's term is 'a secret of God, now revealed.' Here the word probably does not mean a plan of God now made known, since no one understands the speech. It may mean hidden things known to God, or things kept secret to the speaker. (The 'secrets' of 14:25 are a different Greek word, krypta.) The words 'in the Spirit' can be read 'in the Holy Spirit' or 'in his spirit.' The next verses about 'my spirit prays' (14:14) suggest that Paul thinks of both at once, as the human spirit moved by the Spirit.

p: The aulos, a reed pipe, and the kithara, a stringed lyre, were the two main instruments in Greek music.
b: Paul's examples are the Greek aulos (a double-reed pipe, more like an oboe than a flute) and the kithara (a large lyre). Both were played at feasts, in the theater, at funerals and at the festivals of Greek cities. Music in the ancient world followed set patterns of notes, so a player who ran the notes together was not playing a tune. Paul argues from a thing everyone in Corinth knew: a sound without distinct notes means nothing. Tongues in the meeting without interpretation are like a flute that makes noise but plays no melody.

a: a trumpet gives an unclear call
p: In Israel and in the Roman army, trumpet calls told soldiers to march, camp or fight.
b: The Torah has set trumpet blasts to call the congregation and to move the camp (Numbers 10:1-10), and the Dead Sea Scrolls' War Scroll names trumpets for each stage of battle (War Scroll 1QM 3). In the Roman army, trumpet calls were the orders on the field. Paul uses the example of battle because a mistaken signal costs lives. He will use the trumpet again for the last day (15:52). The Plain says 'unclear' to carry the Greek adelon, 'not clear to see.'

a: none of them is without a voice
p: The Greek says no kind of speech is voiceless; most readers take that to mean none is without meaning.
b: Aphonon is 'without sound, voiceless.' It is the same word as the 'idols that cannot speak' of 12:2, where the Plain says 'cannot speak.' Paul's point in 14:10-11 is that a language is something one hears and can grasp, so the usual reading takes 'without a voice' to mean 'without meaning' or 'without a sense that someone can understand.' The Plain keeps the word and leaves the reading to the next verse, where Paul says that if he does not know the force of the sound, he is a foreigner to the speaker.

p: The Greek barbaros is the word that gave us 'barbarian'; it first meant someone whose speech sounds like 'bar-bar.'
b: Barbaros is a sound-word for speech that a Greek hearer could not follow. It does not mean 'savage' in this verse. Greeks used it of all non-Greek speakers. Paul uses it in Romans 1:14 ('both Greeks and barbarians'), and Luke uses it of the islanders of Malta in Acts 28:2, 4. In 14:11 Paul turns the idea against the Corinthians: if they speak in tongues without interpretation, they will be 'barbarians' to each other. A church that prided itself on Greek wisdom would find that insulting.

p: Is the spirit that prays in a tongue the human spirit, or the Holy Spirit?
b: The Greek to pneuma mou is 'my spirit.' Views: (1) The human spirit, the inner self that is moved by the Spirit of God, while the mind (nous) is not involved (Fee, Thiselton). (2) The Holy Spirit praying through the person, as in Romans 8:26 where the Spirit pleads 'with groanings that words cannot say' (some Pentecostal writers). (3) A heavenly or angelic language. Paul does not condemn praying in a tongue; he says he does it (14:18) and he will 'pray with the spirit' (14:15). His concern is that the church be built up, and that the mind not be left out.

p: The idiotes is an ordinary person without training; here a visitor or someone on the edge of the church.
b: Idiotes gave us 'idiot', but in Paul's time it meant a private person, a layperson, someone without training. The phrase 'the one filling the place of the uninstructed' may mean (1) a person seated in a certain part of the room for visitors or seekers; (2) any person who is not able to follow, whatever the seat. In 14:23-24 Paul lists 'the uninstructed' next to 'unbelievers,' so they may be people who are friendly to the church, but not yet baptized. By Justin Martyr's day (about AD 155) the whole congregation said 'Amen' to the prayers of the one leading (First Apology 65 and 67), as Paul assumes here.

p: 'Amen' was the people's answer in Israel's worship; Paul takes for granted that Christian assemblies kept it.
b: Amen is Hebrew for 'so be it' or 'it is true.' In Israel's worship the people answered a blessing or a curse with 'Amen' (Deuteronomy 27:15-26; Nehemiah 8:6; 1 Chronicles 16:36; Psalm 106:48). Paul's phrase 'when you give thanks' (eucharistia) is the word from which 'Eucharist' comes. The Jewish habit of answering a blessing with 'Amen' came with the first Jewish believers into the church, so the Greek-speaking Corinthians had adopted a Hebrew word as their own. The point of 14:16 is that a response to a prayer must be a real one: a person cannot agree to what he does not understand.

a: I speak in tongues, and I thank God for it
p: Paul says he speaks in tongues more than any of them, and Acts never mentions it.
b: Paul's claim shows that he does not look down on tongues. Luke never says that Paul spoke in tongues in his own account of the apostle, though he writes of the Spirit coming with tongues at Ephesus (Acts 19:6). Some scholars connect Paul's words with 2 Corinthians 12:1-4, where he speaks of hearing 'unspeakable words' in paradise; others keep the two apart, because Paul calls that experience a vision. It is also possible that 'more than all of you' means in private, since he goes on to say that in church he would prefer five words with his mind (14:19).

a: It is written in the law
p: Paul calls a prophecy of Isaiah 'the law', and his wording is not that of the Hebrew or the Septuagint.
b: In Isaiah 28 the drunken priests and prophets of Jerusalem mock Isaiah's message as baby talk, and the LORD answers that he will speak to them in a way they will not understand, "with jabbering lips and a strange tongue" (Isaiah 28:11), through the Assyrian invaders. 'The law' here means Scripture as a whole, as in John 10:34 and Romans 3:19. (What 'the law' means in 14:34 is an open question; see the note there.) Paul's Greek differs from both the Hebrew and the Septuagint, and from any other Greek text we have. Christopher Stanley suggests Paul adapted the verse himself; others think he used a Greek form that has been lost. Paul's use: foreign speech, which people cannot understand, is a sign of judgment on those who will not listen. That makes tongues a sign 'for unbelievers' (14:22), but 14:23 shows what the unbeliever thinks of it.

a: a sign, not for those who believe
p: Verse 22 says tongues are a sign for unbelievers; verse 23 says unbelievers will think the speakers are mad.
b: This is one of the hardest puzzles in the chapter. If tongues are a sign for unbelievers (14:22), why will unbelievers say 'you are out of your minds' (14:23), and why does Paul prefer prophecy, which convinces them (14:24-25)? Readings: (1) A sign of judgment: tongues without interpretation confirm unbelievers in their unbelief, as the Assyrian speech did for Israel. This fits the quotation (Fee, Garland). (2) A sign of God's power that unbelievers should heed, as at Pentecost (Acts 2:11-13); but the Corinthians' use is wrong. (3) Paul quotes a Corinthian slogan, 'tongues are a sign for unbelievers,' and then rejects it. All three agree that Paul asks for prophecy, not tongues, in the open meeting.

p: Mainesthe is a word for religious frenzy; visitors may think the meeting is a cult of that kind.
b: Mainomai is 'to rave, be insane.' It is the word Festus uses of Paul in Acts 26:24, and it was used of the possessed followers of Dionysus (as in Euripides' Bacchae). Christians in the first two centuries were often accused of strange rites; Pliny reports to Trajan about 112 that Christians sang a hymn to Christ 'as to a god' at dawn (Letters 10.96). Paul asks the Corinthians to think of the meeting as seen from outside. For him, order and clear speech are a form of witness.

p: The outsider's words echo what foreign nations say to Israel in Isaiah 45:14 and Zechariah 8:23.
b: In Isaiah 45:14 the nations come to Israel in chains and bow down: "Surely God is among you, and there is no one else" (Isaiah 45:14). In Zechariah 8:23 people from every language take hold of a Jew's robe and say, 'We want to go with you, for we have heard that God is with you.' Paul's picture in 14:25 draws on these hopes of the nations coming to Israel's God. The outsider 'falls on his face' (the posture of prostration before a king or God) and recognizes God's presence. Paul writes about prophecy that exposes the heart, not about a sign that overwhelms by noise.

a: a psalm, a teaching, a revelation
t: What a Corinthian meeting was like
p: Paul's list is one of the few glimpses of an early Christian meeting: a free and busy one.
b: Paul lists five contributions: a psalm (a song, perhaps a new one, or from the Psalms), a teaching, a revelation, a tongue and an interpretation. Nothing here says that one person led. Colossians 3:16 and Ephesians 5:19 also show the church singing and teaching together. Around AD 112 Pliny reports that Christians met before dawn, sang a hymn to Christ, and bound themselves to good conduct. The Didache (about AD 100) chapters 10 to 15 shows prophets still speaking freely while also setting rules about testing them. Churches differ today on how far worship should be spontaneous (some Pentecostal and Quaker gatherings) or set by liturgy (Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Anglican), and each points to a different part of the New Testament.

a: let the others weigh what is said
p: The weighing of prophecy is the duty of the others; who the 'others' are is debated.
b: Diakrino is 'to sort out, judge between.' It is the same root as the gift of 'telling spirits apart' (12:10). Who are 'the others'? (1) The other prophets (Fee); (2) the whole congregation (Grudem, Thiselton); (3) those who hold the gift of discernment. Related commands: 'Do not put out the Spirit's fire. Do not treat prophecies with contempt. Test everything' (1 Thessalonians 5:19-21), and 1 John 4:1. The Didache, chapters 11 to 12, gives tests of a traveling prophet: he must not stay more than two days, ask for money or fail to live as he teaches. Weighing is what makes it possible for the church to take a prophet's word seriously without taking every word as final.

p: The same Greek verb is used of the prophets in 14:32 and of the women in 14:34.
b: The verb hypotassetai in 14:32 and hypotassesthosan in 14:34 is the same word, 'be placed under' or 'submit.' The Plain uses 'submit' for both, so that a reader can see the link on which several readings of 14:34 depend. Whether it means obedience to a person, or fitting into an order, is a question each reading answers differently.

a: as in all the churches of the saints
t: Where does 'as in all the churches' belong?
p: The phrase can end verse 33 or begin verse 34, and where it goes changes how 14:34 reads.
b: The Greek has no punctuation. Joined to verse 33, the sentence reads: 'God is not a God of disorder but of peace, as in all the churches of the saints.' Joined to verse 34, it reads: 'As in all the churches of the saints, the women should be silent in the churches.' The King James Version and the NIV join it to 33; the ESV and the NRSV join it to 34; Greek editions differ in their punctuation. For the first: the phrase fits a statement that peace is the rule in every church (7:17; 11:16). For the second: it reads as a claim that the rule is the practice everywhere. Against the second, 'in all the churches' would be followed at once by 'in the churches,' and scholars who think 34-35 were added often count this as a sign. The Plain puts the phrase with verse 33.

p: The Greek gyne is both 'woman' and 'wife', and the same is true of aner, 'man' or 'husband.'
b: The Greek gynaikes is 'women' and also 'wives,' and in 14:35 'their own husbands' translates tous idious andras, 'their own men.' Readings: (1) women in general, in which case the ban applies to all women in the meeting; (2) married women, speaking to or about their husbands (so the instruction to ask them at home makes sense). A puzzle runs through the chapter: in 11:5 Paul assumes women pray and prophesy in the gathering, and in 14:31 'you can all prophesy.' How then can women be silent? The readings of 14:34-35 below, and the card, set out the main ways scholars and churches answer.

t: Eight ways of reading 'to be silent'
p: The rule contradicts 11:5 on its face; here are the main attempts to explain it.
b: (1) A general ban on women speaking in church; the long-standing majority reading (Tertullian, On the Veiling of Virgins 9, among the early writers). (2) A ban on a certain kind of speech, such as weighing prophecy (Grudem, Carson), asking questions, or teaching and ruling (Calvin read it as a rule against women teaching in the public assembly). (3) A rule against disorderly chatter by women or wives (Chrysostom's homily on the passage points this way). (4) A rule for wives in particular, not to interrupt or question their husbands in public (Witherington, Keener). (5) A local, temporary rule for the Corinthian situation (Keener). (6) A quotation of a Corinthian slogan that Paul rejects in 14:36 (Flanagan, Odell-Scott, Allison). (7) A later addition to the letter, not Paul's words (Fee, Payne). (8) A rule Paul himself wrote as a real curb on the women prophets of Corinth, which later readers may judge differently from the way Paul did (Antoinette Wire). See the variant on this verse, and the deep dive in the chapter notes.

p: Paul does not name a verse. The most common guess is Genesis 3:16; some read 'law' as Jewish custom.
b: No Old Testament verse says women must be silent. Readings of 'the law': (1) Genesis 3:16, 'he will rule over you,' or the order of creation in Genesis 2 (the view of many commentators and of 1 Timothy 2:13-14 by comparison); (2) a general Old Testament pattern of male leadership; (3) Jewish oral law and custom, since 'law' in Paul can mean the whole teaching of Judaism; (4) Roman and Greek custom, with 'law' used loosely. Josephus writes that the Torah says a woman is 'inferior to the man in all things' (Against Apion 2.201), a summary of Jewish practice. Philip Payne and Gordon Fee count this vague appeal to 'the law', with no verse named, among their reasons for doubting that Paul wrote the lines.
r: Genesis 3:16; Genesis 2:18; 1 Timothy 2:13; Josephus, Against Apion 2.201

a: their own husbands are the ones to question
p: Greek and Jewish writers of the time give similar advice, and they also give a different one.
b: Plutarch's Advice to Bride and Groom says a wife should speak to her husband or through him (Moralia 142D). In the Mishnah, Rabbi Eliezer says that teaching a daughter Torah is like teaching her 'folly' (Sotah 3:4), while Ben Azzai thought a father should teach her. Archaeology shows Jewish women who held titles in synagogues (Brooten). Paul himself has Priscilla teaching Apollos with her husband (Acts 18:26) and names women as workers (Romans 16:1-7). The instruction fits a setting where questions from the floor, perhaps by women who had been raised without education, were disrupting the meeting. It is also true that it reads as a general rule on its face. The Plain keeps Paul's blunt word 'shameful' (aischron), which belongs to the honor and shame language of Corinth.

a: Or did God's word go out from you?
p: The question can be a rebuke of the whole church or a reply to those who quoted the rule.
b: The Greek begins with e, 'or,' which often introduces an astonished reply: 'What! Did the word of God start with you?' Readings: (1) Paul rebukes the Corinthians for thinking they could make their own rules, apart from other churches (14:33b); (2) Paul rejects the view in 14:34-35, which on this reading he quotes from the Corinthians (Odell-Scott, Allison), so 'or' answers the quoted claim; (3) Paul answers a group of men in the church who wanted to silence the women. The form 'you only' (mounous) is masculine plural, but that is the normal plural for a mixed group, so by itself it cannot show that the speakers are men. In the first view, the 'only you' is the whole church; in the third, it is the men.

p: Paul says that what he writes is the Lord's command; the manuscripts differ on the exact words.
b: Paul uses the word 'command' (entole) of the Lord's words, as in 7:10, 25 and 9:14, where he separates a saying of Jesus from his own judgment. Here he says his rule on gifts is the Lord's command, a claim of apostolic authority over the 'prophets' and 'spiritual' people who were boasting. There is a variant: the SBL text omits the word 'command'; the Byzantine reads 'are commands.' See the variant. In context, the 'what I am writing' most likely covers all of chapters 12 to 14, not only the nearby verses 34 and 35, though readers who see 34-35 as an addition read the sentence with that in view.

p: Euschemonos and taxis are the words behind 'decently and in order.'
b: Euschemonos (the same root as euschemosyne in 12:23) means 'in a seemly manner,' and taxis means 'order,' a military and civic word for rank and arrangement. Paul uses taxis again in 15:23 for the order of the resurrection and in Colossians 2:5 for the church's discipline. In Corinth, with its factions, the closing words restate the rule of the whole letter: gifts exist to build up, and the form must serve that end.
orig: εὐσχημόνως καὶ κατὰ τάξιν (euschēmonōs kai kata taxin)
